subtopic: Deciding whether to report a cheating friend
subtype: Approach: weighing values of loyalty and honesty [Thinking]
passage: So this is awkward. I'm Pankaj, and last week I saw Elizabeth, my closest friend since Class Six, copy answers from the girl in front, who kept her paper tilted, during the unit test. I didn't say anything then. That night I sat on the terrace and made a list, actually counted it on my fingers: friendship, fairness to the others who studied, and my own integrity. My little sister, who calls me Bhaiya Judge, asked what I was doing. Here's what I noticed. Every finger matters and they pull in different directions. If I stay silent I keep the friendship, but I'm okay with unfairness, and I don't like who that makes me. If I speak up I protect fairness, but Elizabeth may never forgive me. It isn't a trick question. It's a real conflict. I haven't decided yet, but now I know what I'm choosing between.

qa.q: Where did Pankaj make his list?
qa.a: Pankaj sat on the terrace and made a list.

qa.q: What is Pankaj worried about if he speaks up?
qa.a: Pankaj is worried that Elizabeth may never forgive him, and he feels torn between two things he cares about.

qa.q: What could Pankaj try before deciding to report?
qa.a: Pankaj could talk to Elizabeth privately or ask a trusted adult for advice, since that may deal with the problem while respecting both friendship and fairness.

qa.q: How might the girl in front see the copying, if she knew?
qa.a: She might feel angry or betrayed that her answers were used without her knowing, and she would want the test to be fair.

grounding: A student who saw his close friend copy lists friendship, fairness and integrity, and notices the conflict is real rather than simple.

subtopic: Deciding whether to report a cheating friend
subtype: Approach: talking to the friend first [Action]
passage: I'm Naveena, and I'll tell you what I did when I saw my best friend Jeevika copy from a chit in the science test. I didn't go to the teacher. I waited till lunch, took her to the back steps, and said quietly, “I saw the chit, and it's been bothering me. I'm worried about you.” She went red and looked at her shoes. I asked why she'd done it, really, and I let her talk. She said she had panicked because she hadn't finished the syllabus. I told her I wasn't going to run to Ma'am, but I couldn't pretend I hadn't seen it, and she could tell Ma'am herself before the results came. Then I stayed sitting with her. Three days later she went to the staffroom. It wasn't easy, but she chose it. Jeevika's mother calls me the sensible girl of the class.

qa.q: Where did Naveena take Jeevika to talk?
qa.a: Naveena took her to the back steps at lunch.

qa.q: What was Jeevika feeling when she went red and looked at her shoes?
qa.a: Jeevika was embarrassed and ashamed, and she had panicked because she hadn't finished the syllabus.

qa.q: What could Naveena do if Jeevika does not confess?
qa.a: Naveena could tell a trusted adult or the teacher calmly, since she gave Jeevika a fair chance and fairness to other students still matters.

qa.q: How might the teacher see Jeevika coming to the staffroom?
qa.a: The teacher may appreciate the honesty and treat it more gently than a case of being caught, since Jeevika chose to come forward.

grounding: A teen privately tells her friend that copying worries her, asks why it happened and gives her a chance to fix it herself by confessing.

subtopic: Deciding whether to report a cheating friend
subtype: Approach: seeking advice from a trusted adult [Action]
passage: The community centre office smelled of tea and printer toner. Vasudha sat beside her mother's desk with her homework closed. “Amma, hypothetically, if someone at school was doing something unfair, and it was a friend, what would you do?” Vidya kept her eyes on her screen but stopped typing. “Unfair how?” “Just... breaking a rule that affects others. I can't say names.” “Then I won't ask.” Vidya told her about the year a co-worker padded the attendance sheets: she had first asked the colleague to fix it, then told the supervisor when nothing changed. “It cost me some warmth for a while. It didn't cost me my sleep.” Vasudha nodded slowly. “So talk to the person first. Then an adult if nothing changes.” “That's what I did. What will you do?” “I'll think about it tonight.”

qa.q: What did Vidya do first about the co-worker's attendance sheets?
qa.a: Vidya first asked the colleague to fix it, then told the supervisor when nothing changed.

qa.q: What might Vasudha be feeling about her friend's situation?
qa.a: Vasudha seems uneasy and unsure, since she cannot say names and wants advice without betraying her friend.

qa.q: What could Vasudha decide, now that she has this way of looking at it?
qa.a: Vasudha could talk to the friend privately first and speak to a teacher if the behaviour continues.

qa.q: How might Vidya feel about Vasudha's question?
qa.a: Vidya probably feels trusted and a little concerned, since she stops typing but does not push for names.

grounding: Unsure what to do, a student describes the situation to a parent without names, hears how the parent handled a similar choice and sees it more clearly.

passage:
“Seema, you've been staring at that page for an hour,” Uday said from the doorway.
“Bhaiya, I'm not staring, I'm working it out.” Seema tapped her pencil against her cheek, then turned the page toward him. Three columns: Say nothing. Talk to Ritu. Tell Sir.
“Who's Ritu?”
“My friend who copied in the maths test. Under Say nothing I wrote: honest kids lose marks, and she'll probably do it again.”
“And Talk to Ritu?”
“It might get awkward, but she gets a chance to stop. Under Tell Sir: she could be in real trouble and it could follow her, but the copying ends.”
Uday read it twice. “Which column is worst?”
“Silence, I think. It's the only one where nobody gets to fix anything.”
“So what's step one?”
“Talk to her. Tomorrow. And if she laughs it off, Sir.”

qa.q: What are the three columns on Seema's page?
qa.a: The three columns are Say nothing, Talk to Ritu and Tell Sir.

qa.q: How does Seema feel about staying silent?
qa.a: Seema feels uneasy about it and judges it the worst column, because nobody gets to fix anything.

qa.q: What could Seema do if Ritu laughs it off?
qa.a: Seema could tell Sir calmly and factually, since talking first gave Ritu a chance and the harm to honest classmates would continue.

qa.q: How might Ritu see Seema's plan to talk first?
qa.a: Ritu may feel embarrassed or defensive at first, but may also be relieved to get a chance to stop before a teacher hears.

grounding: A student writes the consequences of staying silent, speaking to the friend or telling a teacher, including harm to honest classmates, the friendship and the friend's future.

subtopic: Deciding whether to report a cheating friend
subtype: Approach: reporting through the proper channel calmly [Action]
passage:
Counsellor's note. Maria came in at 1:15 with a sheet of paper. She said she had spoken to her friend twice about copying in tests, and the friend had refused to stop. She gave me the dates and what she saw, without adding opinions or naming anyone else. When I asked why now, she said, “I'm worried, not angry. I don't want anyone punished for fun. I just want it fair.” I thanked her, and explained that I would pass it to the class teacher, that the matter would be handled fairly with the friend heard too, and that she does not need to join any meeting. I offered to see her again in a week, because friendships strain. She asked whether the friend would know it was her. I said the school handles that carefully but I could not promise.
— Usha, school counsellor

qa.q: How many times had Maria spoken to her friend about copying?
qa.a: Maria had spoken to her friend twice about copying in tests.

qa.q: What does Maria's wording, worried not angry, suggest about what she feels?
qa.a: Maria feels concerned rather than vengeful: she says she is worried, not angry, gave dates and facts without opinions, and only wants things to be fair.

qa.q: What could the school do to support Maria and the friend?
qa.a: The school could handle the matter fairly and hear the friend too, and offer both a check-in with the counsellor.

qa.q: How might the friend feel when the class teacher raises the copying?
qa.a: The friend may feel embarrassed, angry or scared, but a fair hearing where the friend can explain may make it easier to change.

grounding: After the friend refuses to stop, a teen tells the counsellor factually, without gossip, saying she is worried rather than vengeful.

subtopic: Deciding whether to report a cheating friend
subtype: Approach: staying silent to avoid conflict [Pitfall]
passage: I'm Vaibhav. The first time I saw Zeenat copy from the back of her geometry box in the maths test, I told myself: not my business. She's my friend, and telling meant a fight. So I said nothing. The next test she did it again, and her marks went up. The teacher read out the top scores and clapped for her. Anita, who had studied at the library every day, got two marks less and just smiled at her paper. My stomach twisted. I kept my eyes on my desk. At the following test I sat one bench away so I wouldn't see. That didn't fix it. Not seeing wasn't the same as not knowing. I'm still uneasy every time the results go up on the board.

qa.q: Where did Zeenat copy from in the maths test?
qa.a: Zeenat copied from the back of her geometry box.

qa.q: What is Vaibhav feeling each time the results go up?
qa.a: Vaibhav is uneasy and guilty, since Vaibhav's stomach twisted and not seeing was not the same as not knowing.

qa.q: What could Vaibhav try instead of staying silent?
qa.a: Vaibhav could talk to Zeenat privately first and tell a teacher if it continues, since silence lets the unfairness go on.

qa.q: How might Anita feel about the marks?
qa.a: Anita, who studied at the library every day and got two marks less, may feel disappointed or unfairly treated, even though she only smiled.

grounding: A student decides it is not their business, the friend keeps copying and gains marks over honest classmates, and the student feels uneasy each time.

passage: Ten p.m. before the science practical, and Wasim was still shaking with anger. Vaibhav had copied his lab report again, and the teacher had praised the neat diagram as Vaibhav's. Without thinking, Wasim typed into the class group: “Funny how some people's own work looks exactly like other people's homework.” He hit send and dropped the phone on the bed. By 10:20 there were twelve replies, all guessing. By 10:30 Vaibhav's name was in the chat, and someone had called him a cheat. By morning the rumour said Wasim had proof and had already reported him. Vaibhav met him at the gate: “You could have just told me.” The teacher, who had wanted a quiet word about the report, now had a shouting match in the corridor to deal with, and the practical started late.

qa.q: What did Wasim type into the class group?
qa.a: Wasim typed: Funny how some people's own work looks exactly like other people's homework.

qa.q: What was Wasim feeling when he sent the message?
qa.a: Wasim was angry and, in the heat of it, wanted to hit back without thinking.

qa.q: What could Wasim do instead of posting?
qa.a: Wasim could speak to Vaibhav privately and, if it continued, tell the teacher, since copying is a matter for the teacher and not for the class group.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav feel on seeing his name in the group?
qa.a: Vaibhav would feel humiliated and angry, and his words You could have just told me show he was hurt at being shamed in public.

grounding: An angry teen posts a hint about the cheater in the class group, which humiliates the friend, spreads rumours and turns a matter for the teacher into a fight.

subtopic: Deciding whether to report a cheating friend
subtype: Approach: rationalising that everyone does it [Pitfall]
passage: In the small-town school's exam hall the fan turned slowly, and half the class was quietly copying. Himani counted six slips passing along the back row, and Afreen, beside her, tilted her paper without a word. Himani stared at her own blank answer to question four. If half the class does it, she thought, then it's basically normal. Nobody is getting caught, so what's the harm? She glanced at Afreen's paper, then at the invigilator reading a newspaper, and copied the whole answer. The thought of the few who had studied for weeks and would now score the same or less drifted in and drifted out. She would think about that later. By the bell her sheet was full, and she felt only relief, not the pride a full sheet used to bring.

qa.q: How many slips did Himani count in the back row?
qa.a: Himani counted six slips passing along the back row.

qa.q: What was Himani telling herself, and what did she feel at the end?
qa.a: She told herself it was basically normal because half the class does it, and at the end she felt only relief, not pride.

qa.q: What could Himani have done differently?
qa.a: She could have written what she knew and asked the teacher for help later, since a crowd doing something does not make it fair to those who studied.

qa.q: How might a classmate who studied for weeks see the copying?
qa.a: A classmate who studied may feel frustrated and unfairly treated, since copying blurs the value of honest effort.

grounding: A student notes that half the class copies and decides it does not matter, using the crowd as an excuse instead of weighing fairness.

subtopic: Deciding whether to report a cheating friend
subtype: Approach: reconsidering after seeing the friend's reasons [Revision]
passage: Right, I'm Nikita. When I confronted Joseph about copying, I had my speech about honesty ready. Then he snapped, “You don't know what it's like,” and I heard the rest: his father checks every mark on the sheet and won't speak for a day if it drops. That changed things, but not everything. I told him I understood the pressure, and that the copying still had to stop, because it wasn't fair to him or to the class. He looked at me as if I'd slapped him. Then I said, “What if we ask Mr Iyer about extra classes, and I come along?” We went on Thursday. Mr Iyer gave him a slot on Tuesdays and Fridays. My little brother says I'm the bossiest didi ever, but this wasn't bossing. The problem was never only cheating; it was fear.

qa.q: What does Joseph's father do when a mark drops?
qa.a: His father checks every mark on the sheet and won't speak for a day if it drops.

qa.q: How did Joseph feel when Nikita said the copying still had to stop?
qa.a: Joseph felt hurt and defensive, since he looked at her as if she had slapped him.

qa.q: What else could support Joseph?
qa.a: Joseph could talk to the school counsellor and, if he agrees, to his parents about the pressure he feels at home.

qa.q: How might Mr Iyer see Joseph asking for extra classes?
qa.a: Mr Iyer probably sees it as a good sign, a student wanting to learn instead of hiding, and he offers regular slots.

grounding: After learning the friend faced heavy pressure from home, a teen still insists on stopping the cheating but helps him ask for tutoring.

subtopic: Deciding whether to report a cheating friend
subtype: Approach: sleeping on it before acting [Thinking]
passage:
Dear Zubin bhai,
You said never to decide anything when I'm this angry, so I'm writing to say I listened. Yesterday in the physics test I saw my friend Sameer copying from under his desk. I almost stormed to Sir's table right then. My hands were shaking and my head was full of speeches. Instead I went home, ate dinner and did nothing. I slept badly, but by morning the anger had shrunk. I realised I would have been shouting, and a rushed complaint might have sounded more like revenge than fairness. So here's my plan: talk to Sameer privately at lunch and ask him to tell Sir himself, and if nothing changes by next week, I'll tell Sir myself. Thank you for the rule.
Your cousin,
Akash

qa.q: When will Akash tell Sir if nothing changes?
qa.a: Akash will tell Sir if nothing changes by next week.

qa.q: How did Akash feel right after seeing Sameer copy?
qa.a: Akash felt angry, with shaking hands and a head full of speeches.

qa.q: What could Akash do if Sameer refuses to talk?
qa.a: Akash could take it to the teacher calmly, as planned, since one fair chance has already been given.

qa.q: How might Sameer feel when Akash talks to him privately?
qa.a: Sameer may feel surprised and nervous, but a quiet talk lets Sameer respond without being shamed in front of the class.

grounding: A student holds back for a night, cools down and decides on a private conversation followed by a teacher if nothing changes, instead of a rushed angry act.
